title_en: An invitation for the full moon
body_en: Warm greetings on this full moon day. The full moon is the most significant day in the Buddhist tradition; these are kept as uposatha days, given to wakefulness and meditation.

The full moon of Aadi in particular is joined by tradition to the day the Buddha turned the wheel of Dhamma in his first discourse at Sarnath, and to the day the Sangha was born. It is a fine coincidence that this is exactly the day 6 story in our book.
Let the sangha gather today, and let the quiet of this full moon settle in every heart.
Namo Buddhaya. Jai Bhim.

Niladhamma's 172nd continuous full moon gathering was held on the evening of Sunday 1 February at the Buddha Vihar in Ashok Nagar.

It has been decided that each month's full moon will be led by one member of Niladhamma. Accordingly, this month upasika Priya led and compered the gathering. The event began with Buddha puja. Upasika Gokila explained Niladhamma's journey to those who had come for the first time, and upasika Anushiya introduced the special guest for the month.

The guest was Rajalakshmi, a field worker among the people of Puliyanthope, an MSW graduate working as a programme manager in social service at Don Bosco. Speaking at the gathering she said, 'It was Niladhamma's journey to Deekshabhoomi in Nagpur that gave me my Ambedkarite outlook.'

After those present had been welcomed, those attending for the first time introduced themselves and spoke. The Karumbidari arts troupe played the parai and performed Ambedkarite Buddhist cultural songs and plays.
Several of the newcomers said it was Niladhamma that had given them their understanding of the full moon gathering, and that they would try to come each month. Dinner was given to everyone as dana.

The name we gave him was Nagpur Kala Seth. Affectionately, we called him 'Don'. A man of Nagpur who became family to people from Tamil Nadu through the single call of Jai Bhim.

We came to know him when the Niladhamma family travelled to Deekshabhoomi in Nagpur, and for three years he invited the Niladhamma family into his own home as guests. Not one or two people: 120 of us, every time. Even in a place where we did not share a language, to say that we had come to Sanjay Mishram's house was to be received with a hospitality and a respect that only grew warmer each visit. The auto driver who dropped us off and refused the fare, the baker who parcelled up laddus for us: we have that many memories to tell.

He was caught in a car accident near Nagpur, and despite intensive treatment he did not recover. We attended his funeral on Niladhamma's behalf. In 2023 we returned to Nagpur and, on Niladhamma's behalf, garlanded and paid our respects at the statue raised near his home. Whenever his family comes to Tamil Nadu, Niladhamma stands with them as their own.
Blue salutations, Don. We miss you.

title_en: Sir Alexander Cunningham, father of Indian archaeology
body_en: The British who ruled the Indian subcontinent studied its history and culture in order to understand India. Realising there was no documented history of India as such, they set about constructing one. Among those who did so, one group searched out ancient buildings, objects and records and worked at building up the history of India.

That work brought many difficulties. Because their assistants were largely from the Vedic tradition, there was a constant pull towards giving those studies a Vedic colouring. Beyond that, the places where ancient and archaeological objects and buildings had to be searched for were extremely difficult terrain, and the Indian climate gave the British severe physical trouble.

Even so, with a curiosity that was their own, they went on reconstructing languages that had all but died out, setting the methods of archaeological study straight, building a history through them and publishing it. In doing so they established, on documentary evidence, a great culture in the history of the Indian subcontinent that had been buried under invention. The culture they recovered was Buddhism. The labour of the British officers who did this work deserves to be honoured.

The most important of the many English officers who worked at this was Sir Alexander Cunningham. Appointed archaeological surveyor to the Government of India in 1861, he later founded the Archaeological Survey of India, and for this he is honoured as the father of Indian archaeology. He was born on 23 January 1814.

His studies, which helped recover Buddhism, were published as many books. Among them: The Bhilsa Topes (1854), a history of Buddhism; The Stupa of Bharhut: A Buddhist Monument Ornamented with Numerous Sculptures Illustrative of Buddhist Legend and History in the Third Century BC; and Mahabodhi, or the great Buddhist temple under the Bodhi tree at Buddha-Gaya.

Om mani padme hum. Under the good purpose of a Walk for Peace, nineteen venerable Buddhist monks, together with a faithful dog named Aloka, are walking 3,700 kilometres in 120 days from Fort Worth in Texas to Washington DC, to spread awareness of hope, peace, love, a life lived together, and compassion across the American states and the world.
The walk began at Fort Worth, Texas on 26 October 2025 and passes through Texas, Mississippi, Georgia and North Carolina, covering 3,700 kilometres, to end at Washington DC in February 2026.

Through pouring rain and bitter cold the walk has gone on without a break. Today, 10 January, is the seventy-seventh day and they are still walking. As they cross each city, police vehicles escort them with official honours. People gather along the way, offer flowers, pay their respects, give what they can and offer food, and send them on. Dhamma teachings, Buddhist pujas and suttas are recited along the route as the journey continues.
Namo Buddhaya. Namo Dhammaya. Namo Sanghaya.

January 8, Buddhist Flag Day. The five-coloured Buddhist flag is used in around sixty countries. It was designed by the Buddhist thinker Colonel Henry Steel Olcott. The flag was introduced in Sri Lanka when Olcott went there and held his conversations on Buddhism. Olcott and Anagarika Dharmapala presented it to the Emperor of Japan and to the government of Burma in 1889.

After several revisions the flag was adopted by the Colombo Buddhist committee in 1885, and was first published in the Sri Lankan newspaper Sarasavi Sandaresa. It was raised in Colombo on Vesak day in 1886.

On 25 May 1950 the World Fellowship of Buddhists met in Colombo under the chairmanship of Professor Gunapala Piyasena Malalasekera, the Sri Lankan Buddhist scholar and educationist. Buddhists from twenty-seven countries took part, and Annal Ambedkar was among them. Malalasekera proposed at that conference that the Buddhist flag be made the international Buddhist flag, and it was recognised as such.

The flag has five bands of colour, each standing for a way of the Dhamma. Blue stands for love, compassion and world peace. Yellow stands for the middle way. Red stands for the good effort towards discipline, awareness and attainment. White stands for the untainted Dhamma. Orange stands for the Buddha's teaching and his wisdom.

A sixth colour was in the flag at the beginning, a blend of these five. In the revised flag only the five colours were kept. The five bands also recall the five precepts. That the bands run both vertically and horizontally signifies that Buddhism should spread everywhere and in every direction, equally.

title_en: An Ambedkarite quiz at Margazhiyil Makkalisai
body_en: We decided to run a quiz for those attending the Margazhiyil Makkalisai gathering. On that basis we put together twenty questions, running from Pandithar Iyothee Thass to Babasaheb's turn to Buddhism, and designed the quiz so that it could be answered online in both Tamil and English, and so that everyone who answered could see their own responses alongside the correct ones.
Some of the questions were chosen to set right the distortions that have crept into the history of the Scheduled Caste people.

Many of those who came to the event took part with real interest. Some who had come as a group of friends treated it as a contest among themselves, while others discussed the questions together before answering.
Everyone who answered all twenty questions correctly was called up and given a prize. Anusuya of Niladhamma presented the prizes to two sisters, and Professor Stalin Rajangam presented the rest.
If you would like to try the quiz yourself, you can follow these links. In Tamil: https://bit.ly/ta-quiz . In English: https://bit.ly/en-quiz

title_en: Rao Bahadur M. C. Raja and the “Hindu” identity
body_en: A politics of contempt has been built up in Tamil Nadu around Rao Bahadur M. C. Raja. It would be no exaggeration to say that a campaign was mounted, and is still being mounted, to establish that no Scheduled Caste figure of any standing existed in Tamil Nadu during the time of E. V. Ramasamy.

One of the main charges laid against Rao Bahadur M. C. Raja is that he stood against Babasaheb Dr. B. R. Ambedkar at the time of the Poona Pact. In later years, however, he changed his position and walked alongside Babasaheb.

The video below carries his own view. He says: “If we have no freedom to enter Hindu temples, then we are not Hindus, and if we are not Hindus, why should we join them in a joint electorate?” This is a statement Rao Bahadur M. C. Raja made in 1938.
Source and reference: https://ambedkarambeth.blogspot.com/
At the Babasaheb Ambedkar Manimandapam in Chennai on Babasaheb Remembrance Day.

title_en: The full moon Theri Sanghamitta reached Sri Lanka
body_en: Arahant Theri Sanghamitta, daughter of the Buddhist emperor Ashoka and a bhikkhuni herself, reached Sri Lanka on the December full moon day along with eleven bhikkhunis and a sapling taken from the Maha Bodhi. King Devanampiya Tissa waded into the sea with folded hands to receive her.

The Dhamma had already been taught in Sri Lanka by Arahant Thera Mahinda, son of the emperor Ashoka. Following that, the bhikkhuni sangha was founded with Queen Anula, who is known as the first bhikkhuni of Sri Lanka.

The branch of the Maha Bodhi that Theri Sanghamitta carried was planted at Anuradhapura. That Maha Bodhi flourishes to this day, and holds the distinction, recognised by UNESCO, of being the oldest tree in the world planted by human hand.
Greetings to everyone on Indian Constitution Day.

“The Buddha is a Margadata, a giver of the way,” says Babasaheb Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. Buddhism places enlightenment at the centre. The moral duty of a Buddhist is to reach enlightenment. That is what the Buddha taught.

In that spirit, Dhammachari Gauthama Prabhu gave a Dhamma class to our Niladhamma family on 30 September and on 1 and 2 October, so that we could put the Buddha Dhamma into practice. Following on from that, a Dhamma practice camp was held on 1 and 2 November.

At the camp Dhammachari Gauthama Prabhu taught anapanasati practice, the five hindrances that stand in the way of meditation and how to cross them, how to use a meditation handbook in order to grow in practice, how to take up Dhamma practice together as a kula, the moral duties of a Buddhist, and much else besides.
Our love and thanks to Dhammachari Gauthama Prabhu anna, who guides us to flourish in the Dhamma.
“Reforming Hinduism is not our field,” said Babasaheb Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, and this is the day on which he turned to Buddhism along with lakhs of people. 14 October 1956.
It carries historical weight of its own, in that it is the day on which lakhs of people, bowing to no authority, chose and accepted a religion for themselves.
Let us rise again as Buddhists on the path of Babasaheb Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. A set of photographs from the day Babasaheb took refuge follows.

We celebrated the day Babasaheb Ambedkar turned to Buddhism, and Ashoka Vijayadashami, the day the emperor Ashoka set down his weapons and turned to Buddhism, with a Buddha Puja at the Magizhchi Illam in Siruseri.
The respected Dhammachari Gauthama Prabhu, along with Manish and Ajay, students of the Nagarjuna Institute who are in Dhamma service, took part and chanted the suttas.

title_en: Fifth year memorial for Venerable Bhikkhu Ashvaghosh
body_en: The fifth year remembrance for Venerable Bhikkhu Ashvaghosh was held at his memorial in the village of Nandimangalam in Ranipet district.
Niladhamma and the ABI groups took part, held a Buddha Puja, spoke about their memories of the bhikkhu, and offered a midday meal as dana.

Buddhist chantings are not like other religious chantings. It is not like bhajans or slokas where you praise god or superstitions, or blindly singing, or involving clapping and dancing, or accompanied by musical instruments. It is not a remorseful action or prayer. It is not a religious duty. It is not done for gaining magical powers or supernatural powers. It is not for gaining benefits from god or from supernatural power. It is not to show off your knowledge and talents to others.

Buddhist chanting is a reverential action practised for calming the mind, developing concentration, creating spiritual energy, invoking positive emotions, providing confidence, instilling courage, overcoming our ego, and cultivating spiritual discipline in our life.

During the time of the Buddha, chanting such as paritta (protective), ovada (advisory), udana (inspirational) and sajjhaya (memorisation) were practised. It is purely a psychological and spiritual action for transforming our mind into a higher state of consciousness.
Sadhu, sadhu, sadhu. With metta, Dhammamitra Gauthama Prabhu N.

title_en: Taking refuge in the Dhamma, Friday 15 August 2025
body_en: On 15 August, the day political freedom was won, Niladhamma arranged a ceremony of taking refuge in the Dhamma so that social freedom might be won as well. The event was held at the Arulnilai Buddha Vihar, which stands on the hill at Pallavaram, and began at about six in the evening.

Upasika Priya, a member of the Niladhamma leadership group, compered the event and set out the basics of a Buddhist life. To encourage the families taking refuge, members of families who had already done so shared their own experience of living as Buddhists.

Speaking there, Anusuya of the Niladhamma leadership group said: “Lighting a candle, lighting incense, placing flowers and fruit, all of this is looked at critically in Buddhist practice. Nothing here is compulsory. But some of these things we do only because they agree with science and with psychology. They are used to point to impermanence, and to say: be a light unto yourself.”

Upasika Sumathi, another member of the leadership group, said: “I never believed in god to begin with, so I had no great sentiment about the thali. But when someone kept pointing out that I was not wearing one, without knowing it myself I once carried a fear that something might happen to my husband. After taking refuge at the Buddhist conference in Guduvancheri, that fear left me completely. My husband Ilakkiyan also trusts and keeps to a Buddhist life, so ours is a family that follows Buddhist practice.”

Upasika Kokila, also of the leadership group, said: “Buddhism is being fully aware. Our experience of life comes to us exactly to the degree that we are aware in our speech and in our action. This is a central part of Buddhist practice.”

Speaking as one of the administrators of the vihar, the senior upasaka Ayya said: “The moment we hear that the Niladhamma group is coming, a kind of happiness spreads among us. We come to the frame of mind of people about to celebrate a wedding. They can keep coming and using this place whenever they wish. We will stand behind them.”

Those who took refuge shared their experience, saying they had come to Buddhism to be free in mind and to come out of the ranking that Hinduism imposes on them, and that the feeling that follows brings a rare happiness and contentment.

Upasika Sangeetha of the leadership group had put on display pictures drawn by students on Buddhism and on Ambedkarism, and it drew the visitors strongly. Sangeetha, who had taken refuge at the previous ceremony organised by Niladhamma, read out a poem that moved everyone present.
Groundnuts, tea and fruit were given as dana. Singers of the Karumbidari arts troupe sang and played the parai and gladdened everyone. The event closed at about eight at night.

title_en: Cordoning off Ambedkar memorial in Chennai until CM's visit leads to commotion
body_en: The police's decision to cordon off the Ambedkar Memorial at Raja Annamalaipuram in Chennai until the visit of Chief Minister M. K. Stalin, to pay tributes on his birth anniversary, on Sunday 14 April 2024, led to a commotion, with Madras High Court former judge D. Hariparanthaman himself expressing displeasure over such police action.

The retired judge had gone to the memorial to attend a self respect marriage scheduled to take place at 8 am but found the couple, their family members and friends had not been allowed inside the memorial, citing protocol. They had been asked to wait until the Chief Minister paid a visit to the memorial.

When the former judge explained that the self respect marriage would be over in hardly ten minutes, the police agreed to allow him and the couple alone inside the memorial but not anyone else. However, he wondered how such a restriction could be imposed on family members and friends. Dravidar Viduthalai Kazhagam president Kolathur Mani was also told that he alone would be permitted to enter the memorial to pay respects to Ambedkar.
Aggrieved over such restriction, the marriage between the Scheduled Caste couple was performed outside the memorial after registering a strong protest against the police action.

Addressing the gathering, Mr. Hariparanthaman said: “We are not making it an issue because we do not want this government to earn a bad name on the birth anniversary of Ambedkar. We were prepared to leave the premises before the Chief Minister arrives but it is not proper to prevent us from entering until he arrives.”

He also said: “We have actually been supporting the ruling DMK in the ongoing Lok Sabha poll campaign and had also decided to take the oath, let all of us vote and save the Constitution. This oath was supposed to be taken in front of the statue of the Ambedkar memorial today but now we are forced to take it outside the memorial.”

The judge also recalled that two publishers, K. Senthamizhselvi and Niranjan Vijayan, had filed a writ petition in the High Court that month complaining about a similar restriction imposed by the police the previous year, because of which the general public were able to pay respects at the memorial only for two hours.

Justice S. M. Subramaniam of the High Court had disposed of the writ petition on Friday after recording the submission of the Director of Information and Public Relations R. Vaithinathan that the police would fix time slots and that all arrangements such as drinking water, tents and seating would be made.

Subsequently, when an urgent mention was made on Saturday night complaining that sufficient tents had not been put up, Justice Subramaniam drove down to the memorial along with Additional Advocate General J. Ravindran and the petitioners' counsel A. B. Karl Marx Siddharthar to take stock of the situation.
“The judge came to the memorial at 11 pm last night and inspected the arrangements. Despite all this, the police prevented public entry from 7 am till 10:20 am today,” Mr. Siddharthar said.
Source: The Hindu

title_en: Excavation resumes at Vikramshila University in Bihar after 42 years
body_en: Patna: excavation work has begun again at the site of Vikramshila University in the Bhagalpur district of Bihar, the seat of learning built in the eighth century.

Vikramshila University was built in the eighth century by the Pala emperor Dharmapala. Following Nalanda and Odantapuri, it was built by the emperor Dharmapala to provide education across many fields. It was destroyed during an invasion in the thirteenth century. The university stood in the village of Antichak in what is now Bhagalpur district.
The Archaeological Survey carried out excavation work at the site from 1972 to 1982, which yielded information about many of the important buildings of the university.

Now, after 42 years, excavation work has begun there again. The work started on the eighth of this month, and sand is being cleared from the places already excavated. The survey is expected to yield a good deal of further information about the university.

title_en: A one day fast by Buddhists calling for a ceasefire
body_en: Buddhists came together and undertook a one day fast calling for a ceasefire.

The fast began at 9 am on 18 November 2023. Taking part were the Nila Dhamma group, Bhikkhu Mauriya Buddha, a member of the Tamil Nadu minorities committee, advocate R. K. Devendran, a member of the Salem district committee for minorities and backward classes, a bhikkhu of the Brahmabodhi Vihar and member of the Kallakurichi district committee for minorities and backward classes, and many others.

title_en: The case seeking a public holiday for Buddha Purnima is dismissed
body_en: Many Buddhist sanghas in Tamil Nadu have been making repeated efforts to have Buddha Purnima declared a public holiday. Several sanghas placed this request before Peter Alphonse, chairman of the Tamil Nadu Minorities Commission. We received a copy of the letter forwarding the requests Niladhamma had made to the Chief Minister's office.
The case filed on this matter by advocate Pandiyaraj of Mamsapuram in Virudhunagar district has been dismissed. Our love and gladness to the brother who carried the case forward.

Word came from the schools that 4 April 2023 had been declared a holiday. That day was Mahavir Jayanti. So, although the population of Buddhists in Tamil Nadu is of the same order, a holiday is granted for a Jain festival. This is a moment for us as Buddhists to weigh carefully.

The two faiths that enriched this land in its cultural foundations were the shramana faiths, Buddhism and Jainism. Following Babasaheb's efforts, Buddhism began to recover in this soil, and the arrival of social media has steadied it.

Our present need is this. We are at a point where the Buddhist sanghas working here and there must come together and work with at least a minimum common programme. Each sangha should work on the problems and challenges of the area in which it operates, and joining with the other sanghas across Tamil Nadu on a minimum common programme will strengthen us and open the way to winning our political rights.

title_en: Scheduled Caste people who turned to Buddhism enjoy better literacy and gender equality than Scheduled Caste Hindus
body_en: There are more than 8.4 million Buddhists in India, and 87 per cent of them came to Buddhism from other religions, largely Scheduled Caste people who changed religion in order to escape the oppression of Hindu caste. The remaining 13 per cent belong to the traditional communities of the north east and the northern Himalayan regions. Those who have returned to Buddhism are today also called new Buddhists.

According to an IndiaSpend analysis of the 2011 census data, it is clear that Scheduled Caste people who turned to Buddhism enjoy better literacy, higher employment and participation, and greater gender equality than Scheduled Caste people who remain Hindu. Since 87 per cent of India's Buddhist population came from other religions and most of them are Scheduled Caste people, the analysis proceeds on the assumption that the benefits of the community's progress largely reach Scheduled Caste people.

By the census figures, the literacy rate among Buddhists is 81.29 per cent, higher than the national average of 72.98 per cent. Literacy among Hindus stands at 73.27 per cent, and among Scheduled Castes it is lower still at 66.07 per cent.

“Most Dalits at the senior levels of the administration are Buddhists,” records Satpal Tanwar, leader of the Bhim Army, an organisation now urging Scheduled Caste people to turn to Buddhism in large numbers. “Because, set against the caste system, Buddhism gives them self confidence. It wipes away the humiliations placed on them through vague notions such as bad karma, and makes a way for them to live as people who think for themselves,” he says.

Better literacy rates. Only among the traditional communities of the north east, in Mizoram at 48.11 per cent and Arunachal Pradesh at 57.89 per cent, do Buddhists have a literacy rate below the general population average. On the other side, Chhattisgarh at 87.34 per cent, Maharashtra at 83.17 per cent and Jharkhand at 80.41 per cent have large numbers of literate Buddhists.

The conversion movement is strong in Maharashtra, with Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh also carrying its effect. Maharashtra's story is distinctive, because a higher share of its population than any other Indian state, 5.81 per cent, more than 6.5 million people, are Buddhists. In 1956, B. R. Ambedkar, chairman of the drafting committee of the Indian Constitution, turned to Buddhism along with 600,000 followers. This resistance to casteism continues today. In Uttar Pradesh, 68.59 per cent of Buddhists are literate, above the overall population average of 67.68 per cent and nearly eight percentage points above the figure for other Scheduled Castes at 60.88 per cent.

Better gender ratios. The data show that female literacy among Buddhists in India, at 74.04 per cent, is considerably higher than the overall population average of 64.63 per cent. Only Uttar Pradesh at 57.07 per cent and Karnataka at 64.21 per cent show female literacy below the overall population average, and even these are considerably above the Scheduled Caste figures in those two states.
By the 2011 data, the sex ratio among Buddhists is 965 women for every 1,000 men, against 945 for Scheduled Castes as a whole. The national average is 943.

Buddhists are also attentive to family planning. Children aged 0 to 6 form 11.62 per cent of Buddhists, against a national average of 13.59 per cent. This means that for every hundred people, Buddhists have about two children fewer than the average.

About 43 per cent of Buddhists live in urban areas, against an overall population average of 31 per cent, which also raises their educational opportunities. Around 80 per cent of Buddhists are from Maharashtra, which has better literacy and a higher urban share than the national average. Within Maharashtra, the literacy rate, levels of urbanisation and child ratio among Buddhists are somewhat better than among other groups.
The Tamil words for Buddhism, for the Buddha and for the awakened state all come from the word buddhi, meaning intelligence. Buddhism can be taken to mean being awake.

This philosophy is a way discovered by one man, called Siddhartha Gautama, through his own effort and his own experience. That Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, reached this great knowing, the awakened state of buddhahood, in his thirty fifth year.

Buddhism is a philosophy roughly 2,500 years old. Around 495 million people across the world follow it. Until a hundred years ago it was followed only by the peoples of Asia; today it draws wide support among Europeans, Australians and Americans. From Einstein, the scientist of world renown, to Bertrand Russell, it has stood as a faith spoken of with respect.

title_en: Video of the 127th birth anniversary celebration of Babasaheb Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
body_en: The celebration of the 127th birth anniversary of Babasaheb Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, at the Babasaheb Dr. B. R. Ambedkar Manimandapam, Chennai.
On this full moon the Gautama Buddha, having reached full knowledge, set out for the first time from Rajagriha to Kapilavastu.

The messengers sent by Suddhodana approach the Gautama Buddha. While the Gautama Buddha was living at Rajagriha, word of his gentle teaching of the Dhamma reached the ears of the great king Suddhodana, and little by little a longing grew in him to see the son who now shone as a great knower. As a result he sent nine successive embassies, nine members of his court, as messengers asking the Gautama Buddha to come to Kapilavastu.

Against what he expected, every one of them listened to the Dhamma, reached the state of the noble ones and joined the sangha. From that moment the noble ones became indifferent to the things of this worldly life and did not deliver the message they had been sent with.

Disappointed, the great king finally sent one more member of his court, Kaludayi, a childhood playmate the Gautama Buddha was fond of, in whom he placed complete trust. He too, having obtained the king's permission to join the sangha, gave his consent and took leave. He wondered whether he might also have the good fortune of joining the sangha and reaching the state of the noble ones like the others. Unlike the others, however, he conveyed the message he had brought to the Gautama Buddha and persuaded him to go to his aged father of the royal house.

The Gautama Buddha's journey towards Kapilavastu. Since the season had turned favourable, the Gautama Buddha set out on this full moon day on the long journey on foot, together with his wide following of disciples, the arahants. As the long journey went on, he taught the Dhamma along the way in language ordinary people could easily follow, making no distinction between the poor, the nobles and the very wealthy.

Through the long success of the sangha the Buddha had brought both himself and that noble community to contentment. In his eightieth year the Buddha understood that all his duties were done. He made clear to his earnest disciples, both householders and those who had left the household life, the instructions on practice that could not be set aside. They in turn became firm in his teaching and fit to set it out in detail to others. And so, unwilling to hold his remaining days by force of will, he lived in the full benefit of arahantship.

On the Masi full moon day, while staying at the Capala Cetiya, the Buddha announced to the Venerable Ananda that he would pass away three months from that day. The Venerable Ananda at once recalled what the Buddha had said and begged him to live a hundred years for the good and the flourishing of all. The Buddha answered: “Ananda, enough of pleading with the Tathagata. The time for such a request has now passed.”

After that he spoke of the natural force of a life that passes swiftly, and went with the Venerable Ananda to the hall with the peaked roof in the Mahavana, asking that all the bhikkhus near Vesali be gathered together. To the assembled bhikkhus he gave the following address.

Study well the high truths I have set out to you in detail, practise them, give them your attention, so that this holy life may last and grow, so that compassion towards all living beings in the world may be established, and so that people and devas may grow in virtue and in happiness. Those high truths are: the four foundations of mindfulness; the four right efforts; the four bases of the power that brings fulfilment and knowledge in the life of a community; the five faculties of action; the five powers of spiritual strength; the factors of enlightenment; and the noble eightfold path.

He then made his last address, and made the time of his passing plainly known to the sangha. “Listen, bhikkhus. I speak to you. All things that arise are of a nature to pass away. With awareness, strive for your liberation.” He confirmed that the passing of the Tathagata would come before long, and that the Tathagata would pass away exactly at the end of the third month from that day.
Book: The Buddha and the full moon. Author: Engineer A. Asokan. Publisher: Tripitaka Tamil Foundation, Chennai.

An afternoon five years ago, or to put it exactly, June of the year 2012. Upasakas who were seeking Babasaheb and, on the path he showed, the Buddhist way, sat down together as families and decided that on every full moon day from then on they would gather as families at the Babasaheb Manimandapam and hold a Buddhist conversation, so as to come to know Buddhism. That decision took shape the very next month, in July. The Buddhist cultural group that has today grown full as a moon under the name Nila Dhamma took the first step of its waxing crescent in just that way. The aim at the time was only to gather as families at the Manimandapam.

One of the entertainments that runs without fail through every period of history is the steady blacking out of those figures who cannot be avoided and who answer back to power. Blacking out, in this twenty first century, the peerless figure of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, Babasaheb Ambedkar, and the Buddhism he followed for the sake of a society of equals. Power is doing this with great precision. Building a Manimandapam in the major cities for a leader who has more than a lakh of statues across the country, and then leaving it without upkeep, is one form of that blacking out. To use the Manimandapam that stands in Chennai in a way that works for us was the aim of the first gathering of the Nila Dhamma full moon group.

The moment we take the first step, the path meant for us opens out before us. From the starting point of a gathering, Nila Dhamma moved slowly into cultural ground. It was the women and the children who began to carry that journey forward. Writing their own songs of freedom, staging plays, the children came to know themselves and grew quickly. Buddhism gave them the strength for it.

Once the decision to travel on cultural ground was settled, the next firm decision was to go to Deekshabhoomi, where Babasaheb took refuge in Buddhism along with five lakh people. Growth that takes in our histories correctly is the growth that lasts. Accordingly, the Nila Dhamma group made that journey to the sacred ground for the first time in 2015 with 32 upasakas. The lesson of that journey carried into the following year with 110 upasakas, and it will carry on.

The journey of Nila Dhamma, which opened at the start with songs, plays and arts events, has today set foot in the visual arts as well through a weekly screening, and has begun to spread into every branch of culture. Understanding well that recovering culture is the very ground of the Buddhist revolution, the strong first step the Nila Dhamma group has taken towards it is the Karumbidari arts troupe. However many colours Sanatana Hindu religion paints on her, calling her the goddess of fire or another form of Kannagi, the children of the arts troupe beat the parai for the fight wherever they go, saying that this elder goddess is the first mother of our own line.

Ever so many people gave their support from outside to the small steps we took. From the watchman of the Manimandapam to elders holding high standing in society, this journey of five years would not have been possible without the help of every one of them. To all those good hearts we offer our Buddhist salutations at this moment. Jai Bhim. Namo Buddhaya.

title_en: Ezhudhaak Kilavi, historical experiences that stand in the way, by Stalin Rajangam
body_en: “Those who do not know their own history cannot make history,” says Babasaheb Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. He also says: “The history of India is nothing but the struggle between Buddhism and Brahminism.”

Buddhism flourished in this land and touched the heights in every field, in education, art, literature and culture, and was then brought down by the counter revolution that followed. As Buddhists suffered many troubles and had their history made to be forgotten, those who were grouped as Scheduled Castes lost the history that was their root and lived, and still live, as strangers in their own soil.

It is said that to destroy a community, to cripple it, all you need do is destroy its history. In just that way the history of the Scheduled Caste people has been made to be forgotten, and a fiction has been sown in this soil that they have been the oppressed from the beginning of time, from the moment human beings appeared on this earth. Recovering the history of those people will open the way for them to win their freedom with self respect. That many Scheduled Caste thinkers and writers carry out such important work is no small achievement. Among them, Stalin Rajangam and J. Balasubramaniam stand out.

Stalin Rajangam. From Tiruvannamalai district, Stalin Rajangam works as an assistant professor in the Tamil department of the American College, Madurai. He works on Tamil Buddhism, the history of the Dalit movement in Tamil Nadu, and cultural studies.

J. Balasubramaniam. Born in Tirunelveli district, J. Balasubramaniam took his doctorate at the Madras Institute of Development Studies. An assistant professor in the journalism department at Madurai Kamaraj University, he writes research articles in both Tamil and English on Dalit history and politics.

Books published by Kalachuvadu Publications on 21 May 2017 together with the Dalit Intellectual Circle for Action. Jeeviya Sarithira Surukkam. Stalin Rajangam brought out Ezhudhaak Kilavi, and served as the editor of Jeeviya Sarithira Surukkam, the book published by Rao Bahadur Rettamalai Srinivasan. Suriyodhayam Muthal Udhayasuriyan Varai. Writer J. Balasubramaniam compiled, edited and published a collection of Dalit journals that appeared from 1869 to 1943, under the title Suriyodhayam Muthal Udhayasuriyan Varai, along with Bhulokaviyasan, a collection of the Dalit journal of that name.
Ezhudhaak Kilavi is divided under two headings: history that holds in memory, and history that yields to reading.

History that holds in memory carries six essays. The first, Sindhu, Silai, Sinnam, holds the local history of the struggles against caste. It begins with the way Angambakkam Kuppusamy, who had served in the army, handled the caste fanatic mob that came to attack him on 11 August 1928, and opens out to V. Kandan of Vanjinagaram, near Thumbaipatti, the village where Kakkan was born, and to Rettiyur Pandian.

The second essay, Popular memories that stand in the way of history, describes the work of Ananda Theerthar, George Joseph and Pennycuick. The third, The statues of Kakkan and Shivaji, humility and pride, questions the nature of a society that remembers, in one and the same place, two figures from different communities who worked on different ground. The next essay, T. M. Mani, a Dalit leader, describes the work of a figure born into a Scheduled Caste who came to be known as T. M. Umar Farooq after embracing Islam. The fifth essay, Ponnuthai School, another untold story in the history of Dalit education, describes a school started and run as early as 1952. The essay Pournami Kuppusamy, another unknown figure in Dalit history, notes that the most important of Pournami's activities were his Buddhist ones, and that he ran a journal called Pournami that appeared twice a month, which stands as evidence that this social change is a single continuing run.
All of these essays were recovered largely without any written record, travelling with the memories of people. Stalin Rajangam has put great labour into them.

In the second part, history that yields to reading, the first essay, The anti Hindi agitation, Dalit leadership and Tamil identity, describes the part played by Annai Meenambal, and through her the participation of Scheduled Caste people, and how they were treated in later years.

The essay The sister Veerammal and the brother Veerasamy sets out clearly the working of society, as a comparison between two people born into a Scheduled Caste who accepted and followed Babasaheb's principles and who changed the way they worked to suit their circumstances.

The essay Black legs and the ungrateful, brief notes on the Justice Party and the Congress through the experiences of M. C. Raja, may be called an essential reading for Scheduled Caste people. At a time when the negative events around M. C. Raja and the Poona Pact are all that is widely seen in common opinion and among Scheduled Caste people, the change that came over him later, and the fact that he worked alongside Babasaheb Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, are blacked out, whether knowingly or otherwise.

The next essay describes the Spurtank Road meeting that T. M. Nair took part in, in the history of the Justice Party, and its effect. The essay Nandan and Nandanar, two different currents that shaped twentieth century Dalit political work, describes the narratives around Nandan and Nandanar that circulate in society and their consequences. The closing essay, Dravidian, Paraiyan, Tamilan, describes how these words moved past their meaning as names to settle as social and political identities, and the work they do within the social and political setting of Tamil Nadu.

Ezhudhaak Kilavi, Jeeviya Sarithira Surukkam, Bhulokaviyasan and Suriyodhayam Muthal Udhayasuriyan Varai are rare treasures that recover the history of the Scheduled Caste people. Publisher: Kalachuvadu.
Annai Meenambal was an important Scheduled Caste woman figure.

Her grandfather Madurai Pillai was a well known man of wealth in Burma. The collection of songs the poets sang about him is called Madurai Prabandham. It is understood that for this reason she finished her arts degree in Rangoon before returning to Tamil Nadu.

Her social work is taken to begin with the speech she gave in 1928 in support of the Simon Commission. At a moment when caste Hindus were saying that the Simon Commission should be rejected, and that its intent showed an indifference towards India, Annai Meenambal supported the Simon Commission in order to recover the rights of Scheduled Caste people.

Her father's elder brother, Venugopala Pillai, was commissioner of the Cuddapah municipality, and one of those who organised the Spur Tank meeting addressed by T. M. Nair in 1917. He had connections with Adi Dravida politics and with the Justice Party. Against this background Meenambal too had a link with the Justice Party.

By Meenambal's own account, when Rajaji's government introduced Hindi in schools, C. T. Nayagam of Erode explained Rajaji's action as Brahmin politics, and it was in that sequence that Meenambal began to take an interest in the agitation. That is, from the notes available so far, her involvement in the struggle began as a continuation of the opposition to Brahminism. At the same time it is also the case that the connection later fell away.

From 10 August 1937, when Rajaji spoke of making Hindi compulsory, the opposition to Hindi was carried forward as a campaign by Tamil scholars across Tamil Nadu, and it was when the campaign centred on the city of Madras that the agitation moved to its next stage of picketing and arrest. That is, the agitation turned from the circle of learned people who had carried it in speech until then into a mass movement. Meenambal Sivaraj had taken charge of the anti Hindi campaign in the city of Madras. Meenambal's part was important in turning what had been an ideological campaign of the educated into a mass agitation. Under her leadership a great many Adi Dravidas took part in the protests as anti Hindi volunteers.

Meenambal had the firmness of mind to put a question straight to anyone. One piece of evidence for that firmness is the episode of the fast by Rajamahendrapuram Stalin Jagadeesan during the language agitation. Jagadeesan began a fast unto death from 1 May 1938. At a meeting held in Madras on 10 June 1938, Annadurai said: “If this Jagadeesan dies, what we have to think about now is where to place his body and cremate it. The question is whether to cremate the dead Jagadeesan at the house of the chief minister, or before the governor's mansion, since the governor says he does not care who dies.”

It appears the fast was first begun at the residence of C. T. Nayagam in T. Nagar and later moved to Meenambal's house. Periyar also met Jagadeesan at Meenambal's house. Meenambal exposed the fact that Jagadeesan did not eat during the day but took food at night without anyone knowing. This caused resentment towards Meenambal among the agitators, and put Periyar and Meenambal in an awkward position in which they could not speak to each other. It is understood that in later years Periyar referred to Jagadeesan as a spy of the Congress.

In November 1938, women took part for the first time in the picketing held in front of the Hindu Theological High School. After the conference that followed, the agitation passed wholly to Periyar's leadership.

Annai Meenambal at the Chennai conference. In connection with the opposition to Hindi, a conference of Tamil women was held in Chennai on 13 November 1938. Tiruvarangam Neelambigai Ammaiyar, Dharmambal, Ramamirtham Ammaiyar, Pandithai Narayani Ammaiyar and others took part. Meenambal was the one who did most of the work of organising this conference. Her part in bringing the women of the city of Madras together was the leading one. It was she who raised the conference flag. It was at this conference that the title Periyar was proposed for E. V. Ramasamy by Meenambal and conferred on him.

“The ending of untouchability rests in the hands of women more than of men,” said Babasaheb Ambedkar, who spoke on 25 December 1927 after burning the Manusmriti, and he called Annai Meenambal sister with real affection.

She served as the first president of the South Indian Scheduled Castes Federation. In 1944 she presided over the women's conference of the South Indian Scheduled Castes Federation held in Chennai, which Babasaheb Ambedkar attended. She also presided over the women's conference of the All India Scheduled Castes Federation held in Bombay on 6 May 1945. It is understood that Meenambal recalled how, after that conference closed, Babasaheb Dr. B. R. Ambedkar himself cooked and served her a meal at his home.

Besides being a community leader, she held many posts and responsibilities: deputy mayor, honorary presidency magistrate, member of the film censor board, member of the Madras Provincial advisory committee, member of the labour tribunal, member of the Madras city rationing advisory committee, member of the Madras University senate, member of the post war reconstruction committee, member of the S.P.C.A., leader of the workers of the Parry company at Nellikuppam, director of the Depressed Classes Cooperative Bank, member of the Annamalai University senate for six years, director of the Madras Cooperative Housing Society, member of the welfare society for released prisoners, president of the Gandhi Nagar women's association, chair of the women's industrial cooperative committee, member of the advisory committee of the Madras government hospitals, warden of the Adyar Madurai Meenakshi women's hostel, and chair of the examination board of Lady Willingdon College.
Bibliography: The anti Hindi agitation, Dalit leadership and Tamil identity, in Ezhudhaak Kilavi, Kalachuvadu Publications.
